newsitem.title: USA: Round-the-world balloonist sails over Atlantic.
newsitem.headline: Round-the-world balloonist sails over Atlantic.

text.p: American Steve Fossett sailed out over the Atlantic on Tuesday in his quest to become the first to circle the globe in a balloon, and his flight was going smoothly, his expedition headquarters said.
A cranky heater that had gone out early in the flight was repaired and the 52-year-old adventurer no longer had to rely on a backup unit for warmth in his unpressurized gondola, a spokeswoman said.
"Everything is going well," she said, adding that the mylar-coated balloon lifted by helium and hot air was 70 miles (112.7 km) off the coast of North Carolina at 4:45 p.m. EST (2145 GMT).
Fossett's solo attempt to snare one of manned flight's most elusive records follows failures by British and Swiss teams within the past week.

The Colorado commodities broker planned to ride wind currents northeast to England and then southeast over Europe to Ukraine and then east over Russia, Kazakhstan and China. After crossing southern Japan he would span the Pacific northeast to Washington state and land somewhere east of St. Louis, where he began the trip late on Monday night.

The route could vary, however, depending on the whims of the jet stream. He had air space travel permission from dozens of countries he was likely to pass over but the expedition said not all countries along possible routes had been contacted.

Internet users around the world may follow the progress of his trip at http://www.luc.edu/solo. The site includes Fossett's latest transmissions from the balloon and offers a chance to ask him questions.

His balloon had picked up speed and was travelling about 60 miles (96.6 km) per hour. He was to hold an altitude of from 18,000 to 24,000 feet (5,500 to 7,300 metres) -- lower than two earlier attempts that failed in recent days.
Because his gondlola is not pressurized he will rely on oxygen. Temperatures outside the capsule were likely to be 50 degrees bellow zero Fahrenheit (-45.55 Celsius).

Fossett, who made a fortune in the Chicago futures markets before taking to a life of record-seeking adventures in the air and on water, lifted off on his solo flight late on Monday night from Busch Stadium in downtown St. Louis as about 800 people watched, drifting over the Mississippi River and across Illinois.
He is paying for trip himself, with scientific backup from Loyola University of Chicago.
A similar attempt by Fossett one year ago, launched from South Dakota, ended in failure on the second day when his shredded balloon crashed on a frozen lake in Canada.

A balloon piloted by Bertrand Piccard and Wim Verstraeten went down in the Mediterranean Sunday six hours after taking off from the Swiss Alps. Fumes from kerosene leaking into the cabin brought down the Swiss-Belgian team.

British tycoon Richard Branson and two crew members brought their Virgin Global Challenger balloon down in Algeria last Wednesday less than 24 hours after taking off from Morocco. Their craft had suddenly lost lift and plunged.
Fossett holds a world distance record for a solo balloon flight set in 1995 when he flew from South Korea to Canada.
